title: Indian Diaspora Groups Fight New Four-Year Student Visa Cap That Hits 300,000 Students
excerpt: The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies and other organisations are mobilising against a DHS rule that scraps the flexible 'duration of status' system, effective September 15.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DHS will impose a four-year cap on F-1 student visas starting September 15, 2026.
  • Indian diaspora groups argue the rule creates bureaucratic barriers for students.
  • Grace period for students to leave the US reduced from 60 to 30 days.
  • India's Ministry of External Affairs is actively monitoring the immigration changes.
  • New rule may discourage Indian students from choosing US universities.

  • DHS has finalised a rule replacing the open-ended 'duration of status' system with a strict four-year cap on F-1 student visas, effective September 15, 2026
  • Indian diaspora organisations including FIIDS are opposing the rule, arguing it creates unnecessary bureaucratic barriers for genuine students
  • The grace period for departing after completing studies has been slashed from 60 to 30 days, and mid-programme transfers now require federal approval
  • India's Ministry of External Affairs says it is actively monitoring the situation and communicating with Washington

Indian diaspora organisations are mounting a concerted push against a new US immigration rule that imposes a strict four-year cap on student visas — a move that could force hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals into a cycle of extensions, additional fees, and heightened uncertainty.

The Department of Homeland Security finalised the regulation earlier this month, abolishing the longstanding "duration of status" framework that allowed international students to remain in the US for the full length of their academic programme. Under the new system, most F-1 student visa holders, J-1 exchange visitors, and I-visa holders for foreign journalists will face fixed admission periods capped at four years.

The rule is scheduled to take effect on September 15 and remains subject to congressional scrutiny.

What Changes for Indian Students

India is the largest source country for F-1 students in the US, making Indian nationals among the most exposed to the practical effects of the shift. The new framework introduces several significant changes:

Students whose programmes extend beyond four years — common for PhD candidates and some engineering programmes — must now apply directly to USCIS for extensions, removing universities from their traditional role in managing student immigration status. The grace period for students to leave the US, transfer schools, or change status after completing their degree has been cut from 60 days to 30 days.

Graduate students can no longer change their stated educational objective or transfer to another institution without securing prior federal authorisation, reversing the flexibility that previously allowed students to switch majors or schools without government sign-off.

"International students, many of whom will have spent years in the USA, will now have just 30 days to find an employer to sponsor them or immediately be turned into illegal immigrants. Have these people no understanding of how life works?"

— David J. Bier, Director of Immigration Studies, Cato Institute

Diaspora Groups Mobilise

The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS) is among the organisations opposing the rule, arguing it threatens to discourage talented students from choosing American universities at a time when Indian students contribute more than $8 billion annually to the US economy.

Danielle Goldman, co-founder and CEO of Build, warned the rule would "fundamentally change the flexibility that students have had to apply for Optional Practical Training and Curricular Practical Training" — the work authorisation programmes that serve as the primary pathway from student status to professional employment.

Doug Rand, a former DHS official, offered a blunt assessment: "Most Americans understand the value of welcoming international students and getting rid of needless red tape. This rule would do the opposite."

India's Response

India's Ministry of External Affairs confirmed it is monitoring the situation. Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a weekly briefing that New Delhi is in contact with Washington and will "consistently advocate for genuine students and travellers facing hurdles due to the policy changes."

For Indian students already in the US, the transition happens automatically — their authorised stay will be capped at four years from the rule's effective date. Those in the middle of PhD programmes that commonly run five to seven years face the most immediate disruption, potentially requiring USCIS approval to continue studies they have already begun.

The move comes as Indian student enrolment in the US has declined, with many opting for Europe, Canada, and Australia. Experts warn the new rule could accelerate that shift, undermining America's competitive edge in attracting global talent.
